opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the bear case is worth taking seriously, even though my overall view is that compute will keep scaling pretty fast for at least the next few years.

The core of it is that right now we're scaling compute for frontier training runs at something like four or five x per year, and a large share of that comes from spending more money, not from hardware getting cheaper. Hardware price-performance improves maybe 1.3 to 1.4x a year. The rest is companies putting in way more dollars. You can't keep growing spending at two or three x a year indefinitely. At some point you're talking about a meaningful fraction of world GDP. So the bear case says this hits a wall around the end of the decade unless AI is already generating enormous revenue by then.

That's the first piece: it's a bet that has to pay off. Investors and hyperscalers are spending tens, now hundreds, of billions on the expectation that the systems will become valuable enough to justify it. If you get a couple of model generations that are impressive but don't produce dramatically more economic value, if adoption is slower, if enterprises find it hard to integrate these systems, then the capital could dry up fairly quickly. You'd get something like a bubble deflating. Spending would plateau, or at least grow much more slowly, maybe tracking hardware improvements plus modest budget growth.

The second piece is physical bottlenecks. Power is the big one people talk about. Building gigawatt-scale data centers means grid interconnection, generation capacity, permitting, transmission. Those take years. Then there's chip fabrication: advanced packaging, high-bandwidth memory, leading-edge fab capacity at TSMC. All of these can be expanded, but expansion has lead times, and if demand outruns them you get a period where money can't easily become compute.

Third, there are geopolitical and tail risks. A huge share of advanced chip production is concentrated in Taiwan. A conflict or blockade there would be a massive shock to compute growth, plausibly setting things back years. Export controls and broader policy changes could also slow things down, though they mostly affect who gets compute rather than the global total.

Fourth, and more speculatively, algorithmic returns could flatten. If scaling pretraining gives diminishing returns, and inference-time and RL-based scaling also saturate sooner than expected, the case for the next 10x in spending gets weaker.

So my picture is roughly: through maybe 2027 or 2028, the trend is fairly locked in, because a lot of the capital and construction is already committed. After that, it depends heavily on whether AI has started producing really large returns. If it has, especially if AI is meaningfully accelerating AI research or automating lots of valuable work, then spending can keep going up because the revenue justifies it. If it hasn't, I'd expect a notable slowdown, and that's the bear case. I'd put real weight on it. Not most of my probability, but enough that people shouldn't assume the current trend just extrapolates smoothly through the 2030s.

r001.rationale: The response mentions chip-fabrication bottlenecks and lead times, but does not say AI chip production is growing severalfold annually from a substantial share of total semiconductor capacity or that it would soon hit that capacity limit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the bear case has a few different strands, and it's worth separating them because they operate on different timescales.

The first and most straightforward one is just money. Compute spending has been growing at something like 2.5x, 3x per year for frontier training runs, and that's only been possible because it started from a pretty small base. Once you're talking about individual training runs in the tens of billions, and total AI capex across the industry in the hundreds of billions per year, you're starting to run into the point where this is a meaningful fraction of the free cash flow of the largest companies in the world. To keep going at the current rate, you'd need revenue to show up. And the revenue is real, it's growing fast, but there's a question of whether it's growing fast enough to justify the next doubling, and the one after that. If investors get spooked, or if one of the big labs has a bad year and pulls back, that could slow things down a lot, because so much of this is driven by a handful of actors making correlated bets.

The second strand is physical constraints. Power is the obvious one. Getting multi-gigawatt data centers permitted, built, and connected to the grid takes years, and in the US specifically the grid interconnection queues are very long. You can route around some of that with gas turbines on-site, or by building in places with spare capacity, but it's genuinely slower than people would like. Then there's the chip supply chain, which is incredibly concentrated. TSMC's advanced packaging capacity, HBM memory from a small number of suppliers, ASML lithography tools. Any one of these can become the binding constraint, and when it does, you just can't buy your way out of it on a timescale of months.

The third strand is the one I find most interesting, which is that algorithmic progress and compute growth aren't independent. A lot of the willingness to spend is predicated on scaling continuing to work. If you got a couple of years where the next big training run was kind of disappointing relative to expectations, I think that would feed back on investment pretty quickly. And conversely, if algorithmic efficiency improves fast enough, you might find that the marginal return on raw compute drops, and companies rationally spend less on it rather than more.

Then there are tail risks that I think people underweight. A Taiwan contingency would be catastrophic for the whole picture. Export controls could tighten in ways that fragment the market. There could be a demand shock where a large customer segment decides the economics don't work for them.

Now, I want to be clear about what I actually believe here. I think the most likely outcome is that compute growth continues at a fast clip for at least a few more years, maybe slowing from 3x to something like 2x per year. The bear case I'd put real weight on is not "compute stops growing," it's "compute growth decelerates earlier than the aggressive forecasts, because of some combination of financing and physical constraints, and that pushes out timelines by a few years." I'd put maybe a 25 or 30 percent chance on a substantial slowdown of that kind before 2030. The scenario where compute growth basically stalls, I think that's more like 5 or 10 percent, and it would probably require either a geopolitical shock or a real collapse in confidence that scaling works.

And one more thing that I think matters for how you interpret all this: even in the bear case, we've already built an enormous amount of compute. So a slowdown in growth doesn't mean a slowdown in capabilities, at least not immediately. There's a lot of headroom to get more out of what already exists through better algorithms and better inference-time methods. The bear case for compute is a real bear case for the most aggressive timelines, but it's not a bear case for AI being a very big deal.

r001.rationale: The response mentions rapid compute spending growth and concentrated chip-supply constraints, but does not say AI chip production is already a substantial share of total semiconductor capacity or that severalfold annual growth would soon exhaust that capacity.

astra-6.text:
I think the main bear case is that the spending gets ahead of the economic returns. You can keep scaling compute very rapidly for a while by having AI account for a larger fraction of investment, but that can’t go on indefinitely. Eventually, you need the systems to generate enough value to justify building the next round of infrastructure.

And there could be a substantial lag there. Even if models become much more capable, turning that capability into revenue might require changes to workflows, improvements in reliability, and figuring out how to deploy them effectively. So you could have impressive technical progress and still have companies conclude that they should slow down their spending.

The other part is physical constraints: power, chips, data centres, and the time it takes to build all of those. Those constraints don’t necessarily stop growth, but they could make it considerably slower than extrapolating the recent trend would suggest.

So I’d distinguish being sceptical that compute can keep growing at the same rate from being sceptical about AI progress. You could get a slowdown in compute investment while still getting substantial progress from better algorithms and making more effective use of the compute you already have.

r001.rationale: The response mentions chips as a physical constraint, but does not explain that AI chip production is growing severalfold annually, already takes a substantial share of semiconductor manufacturing capacity, or would soon reach that capacity’s limit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main bear case is that we’re extrapolating from a period where spending could grow much faster than the economy, and that can’t continue indefinitely. You can increase investment from a relatively small fraction of the economy to a much larger fraction, but eventually you need either enormous revenues or investors who are willing to keep funding very large losses.

And there are a few ways that could break down. One is that AI capabilities continue improving, but turning those capabilities into economically valuable products takes longer than people expect. Companies might then pull back on investment, even if the underlying technology is still making progress.

Another is that spending doesn’t translate into compute as quickly as expected. You need chips, power, data centres, and the infrastructure connecting all of those things. Those constraints are somewhat solvable with enough time and money, but they could substantially slow the rate of growth.

Then there’s the question of how much cheaper compute gets. If improvements in chip efficiency and manufacturing costs slow, maintaining the same growth in compute requires spending to grow even faster.

So I’d distinguish a temporary slowdown from a sustained end to rapid growth. A temporary slowdown seems pretty plausible to me. The stronger bear case would be that economic returns disappoint at the same time that hardware improvements slow, so neither rising investment nor cheaper compute can sustain the trend.

r001.rationale: The response mentions chips and infrastructure as possible constraints, but does not say chip production is growing severalfold annually, already uses a substantial share of semiconductor capacity, or would soon hit that capacity’s limit.
